description:
We are the Keplerians, and we come in peace... mostly.  Our mission: to conquer Earth (with clean code and good data, of course). We follow Kepler's laws: we orbit fast near deadlines and slow down only for coffee. 

We're engineering students who love building real software: backend, mobile, web, and a bit of AI. We're looking for teammates who can bring design, frontend, or data skills, and who believe a great idea needs a great demo. Join us and let's turn NASA data into something awesome.

details:
What it does

Field Shift is an Android app with a voice assistant, Eyad AI, who helps Nile Delta farmers decide what to grow and when to sow. He speaks Egyptian Arabic. The farmer taps his governorate on a map, or simply talks about his field, his crops and his sowing dates. Eyad AI asks what he wants most: to earn more, to grow a certain crop at a certain time, or to improve what he grows now. Eyad AI then gives a plain verdict for each option and short advice in the farmer's own dialect: "do this, because of that." Pages on water, heat and salt show the reasons. A second Professional view shows agronomists, extension workers and researchers the same numbers as charts and tables. It includes a regional ranking of 19 NASA data points on a map and a methods page.

How it works

Every number comes from NASA POWER daily weather (1990-2025) for each location. Our engines turn it into decisions:

• Wheat heat: hot days (32 °C or more) while the grain fills, by sowing date, over 35 seasons

• Crop water: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith from POWER temperature, humidity, wind and sunlight

• Salt tolerance: FAO-29 curves

• Crop calendar and income per feddan

NASA MODIS supplies vegetation pictures of the Delta, and MODIS phenology and SRTM terrain serve as cross-checks. One example the app gives: in Gharbia, wheat sown on 1 November meets a median of 4 hot days during grain filling, while wheat sown on 1 December meets 13.

The team writes the advice from templates. A language model may reword it only if every number and key fact survives an automatic check.

Benefits

• No reading needed. In one survey, 31.7% of Delta farmers were illiterate, and most get advice from their sons or TV.

• Works offline. The engines, the advice and 86 recorded voice lines live inside the app. Internet only adds live rewording and extra voice.

• Transparent. Every verdict shows its reason, and the Professional view and the explorer website publish the data, formulas and limits.

Intended impact

NASA's long climate record becomes a decision a farmer can hear and act on, such as moving his sowing date a few weeks to avoid heat during grain filling. Extension workers get a tool that compares places across the Delta, which a chatbot can't do.

Tools and languages

• App: Flutter/Dart for Android, with Dart unit and golden tests

• Data pipeline: Python (rasterio, pytest) for NASA POWER, MODIS and SRTM processing

• Proxy: a JavaScript Cloudflare Worker that holds API keys outside the app

• Voice: Hamsa text-to-speech for Eyad AI's Egyptian-Arabic voice; the phone's own speech recognition for listening

• Language model: Gemini, for guarded rewording of the advice

• Typeface: IBM Plex Sans / Plex Sans Arabic

• Explorer website: shows the data and rules behind Eyad AI

How it is creative

Instead of another dashboard, NASA data reaches the farmer as a conversation in his own dialect. The voice of the advice is generated, but the numbers behind it come from fixed engines, not from an AI.

Factors we considered

• Literacy: voice first

• Connectivity: offline core

• Trust: numbers from NASA and FAO, never invented, with stated limits; there is no yield forecast, and income is a national-average estimate before costs

• Local fit: Delta crops, salt and canal-water realities

• Honesty about AI: disclosed, and kept away from the numbers
